content: The ABCC1 gene encodes the multidrug resistance-associated protein 1 (MRP1), a member of the ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter superfamily. These transporters facilitate the movement of various molecules across cellular membranes. The ABC transporter family is divided into seven subfamilies, and ABCC1 belongs to the MRP subfamily, which is associated with multidrug resistance. The MRP1 protein acts as a multispecific organic anion transporter, with substrates including oxidized glutathione, cysteinyl leukotrienes, and activated aflatoxin B1. It also transports glucuronides and sulfate conjugates of steroid hormones and bile salts. Alternative splicing of the ABCC1 gene results in several variants, but all maintain the original open reading frame. The ABCC1 protein is approximately 190 kDa in size and consists of two hydrophobic membrane-spanning domains and two nucleotide-binding domains (NBDs). Each membrane-spanning domain contains six α-helices. A unique feature of ABCC1 is the presence of a third membrane-spanning domain, distinguishing it from other ABC transporters. The two NBDs exhibit functional asymmetry: NBD1 has a high affinity for ATP binding, while NBD2 is responsible for ATP hydrolysis. This asymmetry is specific to the C subfamily of ABC transporters. The ABCC1 gene is highly conserved, with polymorphisms occurring at low frequencies (<5%). These polymorphisms, often single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), show significant ethnic variation, with some SNPs being unique to either Caucasian or Asian populations. The ABCC1 gene is located on chromosome 16 and encodes a protein that resides on the basolateral side of the plasma membrane, unlike other ABC transporters typically found on the apical side. ABCC1 is expressed in various human tissues, with high levels in the lungs, spleen, testes, kidneys, placenta, thyroid, bladder, and adrenal glands. It is also present in endothelial cells of the blood-brain barrier. Polymorphisms in the ABCC1 gene have clinical significance. For example, the G2168A polymorphism and variants in the 3'-UTR region are associated with an increased risk of lung cancer, particularly in Chinese populations. Individuals with the G2168A polymorphism have a nearly fourfold higher risk of developing lung cancer. Polymorphisms also influence the severity of diseases such as cystic fibrosis (CF) and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). In CF, the G-260C polymorphism in the 5'-UTR region is linked to more severe disease. In COPD, the 3'-UTR T866A polymorphism is associated with milder disease and reduced airway inflammation, while the 3'-UTR G3361A polymorphism correlates with more severe disease and increased inflammation. ABCC1 has been implicated in Alzheimer’s disease (AD) due to its role in reducing β-amyloid accumulation in the brain. β-amyloid plaques, a hallmark of AD, disrupt neuronal signaling. ABCC1, located in the choroid plexus and blood-brain barrier, can transport β-amyloid out of cells. Activation of ABCC1 has been shown to reduce β-amyloid accumulation by up to 80%, making it a potential target for AD treatment. In cancer, ABCC1 contributes to multidrug resistance by transporting chemotherapeutic agents out of tumor cells. High ABCC1 expression is observed in neuroblastoma and cancers of the lung, breast, and prostate. In non-small cell and small cell lung carcinomas, elevated ABCC1 expression correlates with reduced chemotherapy response and lower survival rates. Similarly, in early-stage breast cancer, increased ABCC1 expression is associated with shorter relapse times and poorer survival. In prostate cancer, ABCC1 expression increases with disease progression, conferring resistance to chemotherapy. Animal studies have highlighted the therapeutic potential of targeting ABCC1. In ABCC1 knockout mice, β-amyloid clearance is significantly reduced compared to wild-type mice. In mouse models of AD, the drug thiethylperazine, which activates ABCC1, enhances β-amyloid clearance and reduces its accumulation in the brain. St. John’s wort, containing the active compound hyperforin, has also been shown to increase ABCC1 activity. In APP-tg mice, St. John’s wort extracts with reduced hyperforin levels increased ABCC1 activity by 70%, leading to decreased β-amyloid levels and improved cognitive function.
